title: Attribute Routing
description: Learn to define routes directly on controllers and actions using attributes. Understand how attribute routing provides fine-grained control over URL patterns and how it complements convention-based routing.

blocks.text: **Attribute routing** gives you full control over your application's URL structure by letting you define routes directly on controller classes and action methods using C# attributes. Instead of relying on conventions, you explicitly declare what URL each action responds to.

This approach is especially powerful for APIs, where you want precise, RESTful URL patterns. It is also useful in MVC applications when you need custom or hierarchical URLs that convention-based routing cannot express cleanly.

Attribute routing is enabled by calling `MapControllers()` in `Program.cs` (instead of `MapControllerRoute()`). For MVC applications, you can use both — `MapControllerRoute` for convention-based routes and `MapControllers` for attribute routes.

blocks.title: Enabling attribute routing
blocks.content: Add MapControllers() to support attribute-routed controllers in your application.

blocks.text: The `[Route]` attribute is applied at the controller level to set a base URL prefix. Individual actions then extend this prefix with their own route templates.

blocks.title: Attribute routing on a controller
blocks.content: Define a base route on the controller and specific routes on each action.

blocks.text: In this example, the controller's base route is `products`. The `[HttpGet("")]` on `Index` means it responds to exactly `/products`. The `[HttpGet("{id:int}")]` on `Details` means it responds to `/products/5`. The `:int` constraint ensures only numeric IDs match.

Route tokens are special placeholders in route templates that ASP.NET Core replaces automatically. The most useful token is `[controller]`, which is replaced with the controller class name minus the "Controller" suffix.

blocks.title: Available route tokens
items: **[action]** — Replaced with the action method name (e.g., `Details` → `details`)
**[area]** — Replaced with the area name (used in larger applications with Areas)

blocks.title: Using route tokens
blocks.content: Use [controller] and [action] tokens for flexible route definitions that stay in sync with class names.

blocks.title: Combine tokens with static segments
blocks.text: You can mix tokens with static path segments for expressive routes: `[Route("api/[controller]")]` creates `/api/products` — a standard pattern for REST APIs.
Combining Multiple Routes on One Action
An action can respond to multiple URLs by applying multiple route attributes. This is useful when you want an action to be accessible under different URL patterns.

blocks.title: Multiple routes on a single action
blocks.content: Apply multiple [HttpGet] attributes to make an action respond to multiple URL patterns.

blocks.text: Attribute routing is the standard approach for building REST APIs in ASP.NET Core. It gives you full control over the URL structure, making it easy to follow REST conventions.

blocks.title: A RESTful API controller with attribute routing
blocks.content: A complete API controller using attribute routing for standard REST endpoints.

blocks.title: ApiController attribute
blocks.text: The [ApiController] attribute enables API-specific behaviors: automatic 400 responses for model validation failures, binding source inference, and improved error responses. It is the standard for REST APIs in ASP.NET Core.
Both routing styles are first-class in ASP.NET Core and can even coexist in the same application. Understanding when to use each is key to a clean URL structure.

cards.title: Convention-Based Routing
cards.description: Routes are defined centrally in Program.cs using a URL pattern. Controllers and actions are discovered automatically.
pros: Simple setup for standard MVC apps
All routes visible in one place
cons: Can become unwieldy for complex APIs

cards.title: Attribute Routing
cards.description: Routes are defined directly on controllers and actions using attributes. Each action declares its own URL.
pros: URLs defined close to the code they affect
Ideal for REST APIs and custom URL patterns
cons: Can lead to duplication if not managed well

terms.definition: Defining routes using C# attributes ([Route], [HttpGet], etc.) directly on controllers and actions, rather than using a central route table.
A placeholder like [controller] or [action] in a route template that ASP.NET Core replaces with the actual controller or action name.
An attribute that enables API-specific behaviors including automatic model validation responses and binding source inference.
A URL pattern that follows REST conventions (e.g., GET /api/products, POST /api/products, GET /api/products/1) using HTTP methods to indicate the action.

blocks.title: Convert a Controller to Attribute Routing
blocks.description: Take a convention-routed controller and convert it to use attribute routing with route tokens and constraints.
steps: Create a new BlogController with actions: Index(), Details(int id), and Archive(string year, string month)
Add `[HttpGet("")]` to Index() so it responds to `/blog`
Add `[HttpGet("{id:int}")]` to Details() so it responds to `/blog/5`
Add `[HttpGet("archive/{year}/{month}")]` to Archive() so it responds to `/blog/archive/2024/01`
In Program.cs, ensure `app.MapControllers()` is called to enable attribute routing
Run the app and test each URL pattern in the browser
blocks.expectedOutcome: `/blog` shows the blog index, `/blog/5` calls the Details action with id=5, and `/blog/archive/2024/01` calls Archive with year="2024" and month="01".

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: Attribute routing defines routes directly on controllers and actions using C# attributes
Enable attribute routing with `app.MapControllers()` in Program.cs
[Route("products")] on a controller sets the base URL prefix for all actions
Route tokens like [controller] automatically insert the controller name into the URL
Multiple [HttpGet] attributes on one action make it respond to multiple URL patterns
Attribute routing is the standard for REST APIs, often combined with [ApiController]
blocks.takeaway: Attribute routing gives you precise, declarative control over your URL structure. For APIs it is the standard approach; for MVC applications it complements convention-based routing for custom URL patterns.
